taxonomyNote: Animal Diversity Web files this species as Cnemidophorus tigris/western whiptail; NatureServe uses Aspidoscelis tigris, Tiger Whiptail, and notes that some authorities treat the marbled whiptail (A. t. marmorata) as a separate species.
fieldMarks: Slender lizard 127-330 mm total length with a triangular head, slim body and long tail.
Light brown or orange ground colour with eight light or dark longitudinal stripes from head base to tail, plus small black or white spots on the back.
Males slightly larger than females; juveniles are light orange with dark spots or stripes.
Similar to sympatric whiptails; the all-female New Mexico whiptail is smaller with a blue tint on the belly and tail end.
behavior: Diurnal, active forager that digs for prey and uses chemical senses; active mainly April-September in the north, with juveniles active longer.
Uses rodent burrows or digs its own, and shelters in burrows overnight and in inclement weather.
Insectivore; grasshoppers, beetles and termites are frequent prey in New Mexico.
habitat: Deserts and semiarid shrublands with sparse vegetation, plus open woodland, dry forest, canyons and riparian areas on firm, sandy or rocky soil.
Shelters in burrows or under surface objects; eggs are laid underground.
range: Oregon and Idaho south through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado and western Texas to Baja California and northern Mexico.

lookalikes.name: New Mexico whiptail
lookalikes.howToTell: Female-only species, smaller than the western whiptail, with a blue tint on the underbelly and tail end.
